The SmartUp Way

SmartUp Foundations Course - Lecture 10

Given November 3rd, 2024 by Yonatan Stern

So, first of all, thanks to everybody who came here. We have a full house today, so thank you. This is the 10th lecture, which surprises me — how much we've covered. And I wanted to touch on something very basic, which is why startups fail. We all say, nine out of ten startups fail, and we take it kind of like, yeah, that's what happens. It's difficult, blah blah. But what I would like to do this time is dive into the details of why so many companies fail along the way. And is it a law of nature, or maybe something can be done about it to increase the chances of success. So, as usual, we'll introduce ourselves. Ayala and Libby sit over there — for those of you who don't know who they are. Ruthie is hiding. Here is Ruthie. And we're going.

And as I always say, what we have here is basically teaching the profession of building successful companies. It is a profession. I keep insisting on it. It can be taught, it can be practiced — it's a methodology. And as you will see today, I'm looking at what happens if you don't follow the methodology and what happens when you do. The foundation course talks about successful companies. We define what a successful company is, and we have three parameters for it. First and foremost: profitable. If it's not profitable, it's going to die. Second: fast-growing. Just being profitable like a small store and going from day to day — that's not very interesting. It has to be fast-growing. And the last one is growing fast from internal resources, which means modest investment. We're planning to do workshops,

— that was my daughter — and we're going to cover specific subjects there. The plan we're doing here is a residency program, because very much like teaching any other profession, you need to practice it. So if you study to be a civil engineer, a mechanical engineer, an electrical engineer — whatever it is — you finish the Technion or MIT, doesn't matter, and you kind of know nothing. That's the reality. So you go to work for a company for four, five, six years. You specialize in something, and that's when you become a professional. The only exception is startups. You have a great idea, you have an algorithm in your head, it's phenomenal — and you have no clue about how to build a company, yet you get $20 million and someone says, go build a company.

And you really have no idea what you're doing. So that's what we're trying to change here — to teach you how to do that and work with you on a daily and weekly basis. As somebody taught me: when you give a lecture, tell them what they're going to hear, then tell them, then tell them what you told them. Right? So you will have to tolerate me. What we're going to do is follow the life of a typical first-time entrepreneur. There's nothing simpler than that — let's just go look at what's going on. Those of you who've built a company, I'm sure you'll recognize many of the things I'm going to say. And those of you who haven't, it's going to be interesting.

So we're going to follow the process of fundraising — from angel investors to venture capital firms — and explain the whole ecosystem of venture capital and its impact on companies. We touched on that in the first lecture when we talked about how venture capital firms are built. I'm not going to repeat that. I'm going to talk about different aspects of the venture capital ecosystem. Those of you who want that material, go back to our website, look at the first lecture, and you'll see how venture capital firms work. We're going to talk a lot about the mathematics of fundraising, dilutions, and how it all works. It's going to be a little bit of math. Those of you who are afraid of it — just go to sleep, you won't miss anything.

But those of you who really want to understand how fundraising works, how you get diluted or not diluted, what participating preferred is and what common stock is — I'm going to cover that so you have that knowledge as well. And then we'll talk about the tightrope walk. You don't have a profitable company, which means you need to raise money all the time — and what happens when you walk that tightrope while building a company. Very much like an actual tightrope — you're standing up there, and I've never done it because I'm afraid of falling. And I'm sure all of you are afraid of falling too. So that's it.

We're going to analyze this later, after we look at the case study I'm going to walk through. We'll analyze it and then talk about what we recommend doing. We'll compare and contrast — show how a typical startup operates, then show what we recommend and why founders who follow this startup methodology have two things working for them. First and foremost, they have a much higher probability of being successful — meaning building a company that is sustainable, growing, and doing well. And second, they're going to make more money out of it because they're going to own a much bigger share of the company than in a VC model. And anything written in red is a question.

So since this is a fairly complex subject and many of you have lived through it, feel free to ask questions. I'll try to stop every 15 minutes or so and ask if there are questions. But if you have a question, just raise your hand — I think it'll make the lecture more interesting. Okay, so Mitch, I hope you recognize this guy. There is a website called "This Person Does Not Exist." This is one of those — I liked him though. He looks smart. And he's a top-notch engineer with a great disruptive idea. He has a solution for complex online mental health services — matching providers, psychologists, social workers, and others with people who need help, but doing it online.

The reason I chose this is: A, we played with it a little and you'll see that at the end, and B, Russ Glass — who used to be VP of Marketing at ZoomInfo — later built Bizo. We sold Bizo to LinkedIn, and then he went and became the CEO of a company called Ginger.io. And that's what they were doing. So I have information from both sides.

— Sounds like a Netflix series.
— Yeah, almost.

So he did the first thing — Joe, he quit his job. He committed. He has enough savings to live for six months without a salary, a little bit of savings, and friends and family said they can support him a bit. So he thinks he has another $20,000 to $50,000 to invest in building his dream. That's where he is: left his job, can live for six months, has a little money, and wants to build a company. Who here has been in that situation? So it's his first time. And what is he going to do now?

The reality is he's lost — like many first-time founders. He left his job, he has his dream, but he doesn't know what to do. He has a very clear vision of the application — all the buttons, exactly how it's going to work, how people are going to sign up for it, all of that. He's an engineer, but he has no idea how to raise money, how to hire a team, how to develop a product. He needs help. That's the situation of most first-time founders. So he looks for a co-founder. Why do you want a co-founder? You see it's in red — that's a question I'm expecting an answer to. Why do people take co-founders?

— Right.
— Okay, good. What else?
— Share the risk.
— That's it. You don't have any co-founders here?
— Yeah, that's correct.
— What else?

Okay, so I'll do the work for you. Exactly. When I ask people — and I ask a lot of people who came with co-founders — why did you go with a co-founder? The answer many times is the first one: "I was lost, I was sitting alone at home, I didn't know what I was doing, it was very difficult. So I wanted somebody to be—"

— To get lost with me.

Exactly. Be with me. We can do it together. And since I didn't have money, I couldn't hire them — so that's what I did. Second is what you said: complement my skills. I'm an engineer, so I should probably take a business person, someone with more experience. And the other thing, which is very critical: when you go to a venture capital firm to raise money and it's only you, they say no — especially the first time. They don't like it. If I went to a VC, I'm sure they would give me money, but I don't need their money — it's like a bank that gives you a loan only when you don't need the loan. But if you do need it and you don't have money, it's a problem.

You need a team in order to raise money. From their perspective, if you couldn't bring a co-founder, you might not be able to build the team either. So here are all the reasons why people bring co-founders — maybe there are more, but these are the main ones. Okay, so how do you choose a co-founder? Someone you trust? Okay. Define what you want from your co-founder. I'll tell you the truth — there are two ways. One is you've known the person for a long time. You were at another company with them for ten years, you worked closely together, you went to kindergarten with them — that kind of thing. The other is you don't know the person and you start asking around. Remember, you're not a company — you have no money, you can't hire a recruiting firm. So what do you do? You ask a small, random circle of acquaintances. So Joe met Julie — she's his neighbor's college roommate.

— She doesn't exist.

She doesn't exist. But I liked her, so I put her here. Okay, so now we have Julie. And she does have something going for her — she has an MBA from Harvard. If you want to raise money, that tells you something. Hopefully she's really smart and knows what she's doing. She has an MBA from Harvard and she was a VP of Sales — because remember, he's an engineer who wanted someone with business and sales experience. She worked as VP of Sales at a company where, nine out of ten times, it failed. And as a co-founder, she gets 50% of the company. He doesn't know what he's doing, she doesn't know what she's doing — so 50/50. If anybody thinks I'm saying something stupid, please stop me. But you're all laughing because you know it's the truth. It is the truth. So let's just be realistic — that's what happens.

So he picked his neighbor's college roommate — remember that — and gave her 50% of the company. Now Joe owns 50% of the company, and they start a company. They came up with a great name: Theriva. And look at the logo. For those of you who can see — there's a little tool here called Namelix. I strongly recommend that site. It's very creative about inventing company names and generating logos. If you want to start a company, in five minutes you'll have a great name and a logo. So anyway, we just started Theriva, we have a logo, and we are very happy.
And look at the logo. So those of you who can see — there's a little thing in here called Namelix. I strongly recommend this site. It's very creative about inventing company names and giving you logos. So if you want to start a company in five minutes, you'll have a great name and a logo. So anyway, we just now started Theriva and we have a logo and we are very happy.

Okay, so let's talk about the typical order of activities. Now that we have a team, we have a name, we have a logo — it's time to raise money. So we need to prepare a pitch deck. What is a pitch deck? A pitch deck is the story we tell investors of why putting money with us will be the best thing they've ever done. So we're going to go step by step. Julie knows because she was at Harvard — she knows how to write a pitch deck. And it looks like this: the problem the company targets is mental health care. It's a disruptive solution. I've never seen a pitch deck that doesn't have the word "disruptive" at least on every other page. Because it's an online service, it's much more accessible, right?

You can be anywhere in the world and get the help you need. And it's more affordable — that's what they claim. Because they believe that delivering this service online will be much more affordable. Potential market size — jokingly, I said it must be at least a billion dollars, right? Probably bigger. And you always put some market research in there. She's in Harvard MBA, she knows how to get the market research, and she proves the market is probably $10 billion. They put in the competition, the team — which is themselves — and the logo, and they put in financial models. I'm going to show you three examples of financial models. They don't relate to Theriva because I didn't have patience anymore. But they all look the same. They have this shape at the beginning — it goes flat and then boom. All right, so we'll see the boom.

Here it is. Okay. Financial plan. Here's another one. I just copied them from the web — not necessarily interesting. They all look the same, by the way. Doesn't matter. They all look the same. Okay, so they went to raise money and succeeded, because they look good, they know what they're talking about. And they were able to raise $1 million in a seed round. And they only had to give away 20% of the company's equity for this seed round. Okay — $1 million, 20% of the company. Until now, we are thriving with Theriva. Okay, so what do we do now? We hire a team, right? That's what you do. You have a clear idea of the product you want to build — now it's time to start delivering. So they hire a team. Two founders, Joe and Julie.

Now they want to get a salary — five engineers to write the code. They also hired two licensed psychologists because they're developing a platform for psychologists, so they wanted to have them in-house to help with the design. A product manager, obviously, an office manager, and they rented an office. Where's the money? A billion dollars? Oh no — you serious? Right? $100,000 a month goes just like that, but that's what's expected. And the money in the bank will last less than a year. Because you take a million divided by 100,000, you get about 10 months. So you need to start going after Round A. Who here has had a startup? Raise your hands. Okay. How often do you go and raise money? Right? So you start getting into this trap. Okay, but this time they said, we raised seed financing — we're going to go and raise money from venture capital.

Okay. Good times to raise money. So now I'm going to give you a little understanding of how the venture capital ecosystem works. Remember the first lecture where we talked about their internal finance? You know, they get 2% management fees and all of that stuff. This time I'm going to talk about the ecosystem altogether. So when are the good times to raise money? In the life of a company, there are points in time where it's easy to raise money and there are points in time where it's very hard. So what are the times when it's easy? Easy — kind of. So the concept stage, right — like at the beginning when they went to the seed round. You have a concept, okay. You have a good team — Harvard MBA and a good engineer — and you have an interesting, disruptive idea. You're going after an interesting market and you have this hockey stick. You look interesting. And there's no real measurement to assess how much you're actually worth, because the market is $10 billion. You look great. I specifically chose good-looking people, you know — they look good, they look professional. How much are they worth? I don't know. So you go with them, right? $5 million, whatever. Close — but you'll see that you were wrong. Proof of concept accomplished. So that's the first time you can raise money. Can you raise money when you're in the middle of development? Not really, because you're in the midst of something and there's nothing to show for it.

So the next point in time where you can raise money is when you have a working prototype or a product. You have something to show for the money you raised the previous time. You have to understand that raising money has very specific milestones. You can't raise money whenever you want — there are milestones. If you meet a milestone, you can raise money. If you don't, people will talk to you and be polite, but won't do anything. They want proof of the pudding. Okay, so that's the second milestone. Third milestone is early traction. You have a few beta users, they're using it, they give you good feedback, and investors can talk to them — that's the most important thing. Until now they had nobody to talk to. Now they can call the beta users and say, "What do you think about this product? Would you use it? Would you recommend it?" So there is a milestone there.

Yes. Why?

It's not the same stage.

Because even if you have a product without beta users — let's say it's a complicated algorithm or something — you have something to show for. Okay, so many times there is a product development milestone. Think about recycling — you want to show them that you can recycle a certain plastic or something. You don't have any customers, you don't have any beta users, but you can prove that the process works. Okay. Early traction — you have those users — and then the product launch. So you went from beta and now you sell the product. You have a few customers to show for. Again, investors can now call those customers and say, "What made you pay $20,000 for this?" And get an answer like, "Oh, it helps me here, it saves me money." Remember, these milestones are milestones of validation for investors — each one lets them say, "Yep, the risk is lower because they've hit another milestone." And then the last one is when you have a proven sales process. That means you know how to sell one deal after another — it's not five early customers you scraped together somehow. This is much more like a repeatable process. Okay. Yes.

On the previous slide, the fourth point has "several customers" — how many is that exactly? How do you measure it?

You don't, really. No — let me explain. Okay. Remember, you're trying to raise money. You follow what the VCs ask you to do. If you finish beta and you don't have a single paying customer, they'll say, "Why is nobody paying?" You have two paying customers and they ask why not three. You'll see the problem in a moment — there's a funny little video I brought up. My point is: it's never enough. It's never enough. You'll see it. Okay, so what happens between the milestones? What happens between the milestones is what's called the death zone — which means you can try to raise money, VCs will be very polite, they'll drag you along, but basically they're saying, "Come back before you bring me five paying customers. It's interesting — it's really interesting." So basically, it's in between. The development phase: from concept stage to working proof of concept, from working proof of concept to product with beta users, from beta users to early paying customers, from first customers to a working sales process. And the last one — when you really want to get high valuations — you have to prove that you have a growth engine, meaning you've figured out how the thing is going to grow like crazy. The reason you're still raising money at that stage is often that the growth engine is very expensive. So it's not necessarily that having a growth engine means you're making money. I'll give you an example.

If you're giving access to your application for free — like Facebook or LinkedIn — you're measured by the number of users, because everybody understands that your revenue is going to come from advertising. But you have to prove that you're going to reach 100 million users or 500 million users. So growth trajectory is different from making money and being profitable right away. On that, I personally tend to believe you should be profitable all the time. But — okay, so I want to show you the video I promised.

Our hosting fees could become a challenge as we scale, right?

But we can offset a lot of that once we get a few customers and start a subscription revenue model.

No, no, no, no — no revenue. I'll call you back.

What?

Why would you go after revenue?

To make money.

No. If you show revenue, people will ask how much — and it will never be enough. The company goes from being a 100x or 1000x play to a 2x dog. But if you have no revenue, you can say you're pre-revenue. You're a potential pure play. It's not about how much you earn — it's about what you're worth. And who's worth the most? Companies that lose money. Pinterest, Snapchat — no revenue. Amazon lost money every quarter for the last 20 years, and Bezos is king.

The king.

No revenue. No one wants to see revenue — go.

I just thought the goal of companies was to make money.

Yeah, no — that's not how it works. I don't want to make a little bit of money every day. I want to make a ton of money all at once. ROI. ROI. You know what that stands for?

Return on investment?

Nope.

Radio on Internet.

Thanks to Ruti who found that video — I think it explains it much better than I ever could. All right, so back to the boring stuff. So that was one side, right? The other side is that the venture capital market goes through cycles like everything else in business. There are hot periods and cold periods. Obviously in the cold periods it's hard to raise money, and in the hot periods it's easy. So from 2000 to 2024 — I looked at 24 years to give you a sense. From 2000 to 2003 — I had two startups at the time — the year 2000 came around and the dot-com bomb hit. And I was pretty worried about the inability to raise any money at that time.

So I was running Cardscan and we laid off a third of the people right at the beginning of 2000 because I was so scared we were going to run out of money — and there was no way to raise money during that period. It was literally a desert. You couldn't raise a penny. 2008 — you're not that young, so many of you do remember 2008 — the global financial crisis: can't raise money. 2016–17, there was a brief cooling period. And now — right, so all of you know that now is not a great time to raise money either. So if you look at this 24-year period, about half the years were cold years, half the years —
Speaker: So you couldn't raise a penny at that time. 2008 — you're not that young, so many of you do remember 2008, right? The financial crisis, you couldn't raise money around the world. 2016-17 there was a brief cooling period, and now — well, all of you know that now is not a good time to raise money. So if you look at this 24-year period, half the years were cold years.

So if you are going to raise money randomly, there is a good chance you will be in the cold period, not the hot period. So let's look at the hot period — not surprisingly, it's the other years. 2004 to 2007, the Web 2.0 boom. Remember that? 2000, the dot-com bomb. Then it comes again — cycles, always cycles — 2011 to 2015. After the 3G iPhone and Android, suddenly the whole mobile communications area became really interesting. 2018 to 2021, huge boom. Huge boom. I liked especially the unicorns — companies that do nothing and are worth a billion dollars and up. Those mythological horses were roaming the streets out here. I looked out the window and saw them many times going down the street, but whenever I tried to catch one, I couldn't. So that's the cycle, and let's take another look at what they invest in.

When you're trying to raise money, you have to be attractive to venture capital firms, right? It's not enough that you are nice and have an MBA from Harvard — are you doing something that is of interest to VCs in general? VCs go in herds. If they all decide that something is interesting, they will all go after that thing, and if it's not in that category, they won't touch it. So in 2000–2010, enterprise software was very big. I remember that. Cleantech — nobody talks about cleantech today. Early social media started, and mobile infrastructure again. As I described, 2011–2020 it was consumer mobile apps, iPhone, Android, SaaS, cloud services, fintech, and AI started to show up — especially after 2016, when people realized it really works. That's when it started taking off. Remember, we are now eight years later.

So just think about the time it takes for things to really scale up. Digital health, e-commerce, and remote work — you can read the rest, but this is more relevant to the COVID period. I'll mention it — I took this from ChatGPT. I verified it has a good source, but I'm not responsible beyond that. At least there's a source I trust.

Consistently challenging sectors — remember these, because if you want to raise money and you are in one of these sectors, you're going to have a hard time raising money even if you have a good idea. Hardware — though AI chips obviously are very hot right now, so even though hardware in general is cold, that segment is hot. Capital-intensive manufacturing — nobody wants to manufacture anything anymore. Traditional retail, non-tech-enabled services, deep tech. Deep tech used to be the darling of many venture capital firms, but nowadays they say no — it takes too long, too risky, we don't want to invest in it. Next week that might change.

So this is all what they decided at that moment. But here's the challenge — the company is not profitable, as you said, they keep spending money, so they need to continually raise money. Raising money depends on four things: the company stage — remember we talked about the death valley curve — and this is something I haven't brought up yet. When investors look at a company, one of the things they look at is the team. At the beginning it's enough that they have a Harvard MBA and all that good stuff, but later on they start looking deeper. How do they work together? They ask the board what it's like to work with these people. Usually the board is heavily involved in raising money because it's investor to investor. So having a good relationship with the board is critical. Having a good relationship with the previous investor is critical. Having a good relationship within the company — all of that suddenly becomes very critical. Remember the saying: once you can measure something, everybody looks at it. So now they can measure how the team works, and they look at it.

The second thing is the industry and market cycle. If you come at a cold moment — like 2008 — nobody is going to put in money even if you are really exciting, because remember what they do have: they have the companies they already invested in that they need to keep supporting, otherwise they will lose them, and they don't make new investments. That's the way it works. And the last factor is what the market is focused on at the time. So you might have started with cleantech, which was very hot, and by the time you've developed the product and have the process in place, nobody's interested in it anymore.

So what you start seeing is what I'm calling the tightrope that we discussed before. You really have to time what you do, and if you don't time it right, you're in trouble. And the conclusion is: if you are able to raise money, take as much as you can. It doesn't matter — if they are willing to give it to you, take it. Money in your bank is much better than money in their bank.

Audience member: Depends on who you're asking.

Speaker: For you. For you. Okay, so if you are in the process of raising money and you came to raise $2 million and you have oversubscription — that's what it's called — and you can raise $10 million, take the $10 million. Yes, you're going to be diluted, but when times are bad and you need the money, you're going to be diluted much more.

Audience member: But then you reach profitability after a much longer time compared to—

Speaker: If you take only the $2 million — and if you're smart, you put it in the bank and you don't touch it — profitability has nothing to do with it. It's an investment, not a loan, so it has nothing to do with it anyway.

So remember, they are first-time founders and they raised $1 million. They have a small team, they're in the product development stage, and expenses are about $100,000 a month. So they need to raise money, and the timing worked out — it was really phenomenal timing — and boom, they raised $5 million from a venture capital firm called High Flying Ventures. I was very creative last night. High Flying Ventures, at a pre-money valuation of $10 million. So the pre-money valuation went up 50%. The round dilutes the founders by 33%. I'll explain that later — I'll give you all the formulas, don't worry. And Joe, the founder of the company, now owns about a quarter of the company.

High Flying Ventures wants to accelerate the company's growth. They say, "Hey, I gave you $5 million — do something with it." Those of you who have ever raised money know the story. Stop laughing. Yeah, I know — I used you as an example. You're not embarrassed. That's what everybody does. Literally everybody does the same thing.

So what do they do? The team grows to 20 people, expenses grow to $350,000 a month, and within a year they're successful. They have a product in beta — they're really doing well, doing what they said they were going to do.

A 20-person team is not that big. Life looks good, they're moving. But $350,000 a month over a year is close to $5 million. So they now need to go and raise money again. And if you think I'm joking, I'm not. Anyone here with a little bit of experience knows that's what VC-backed companies do. The CEO is doing one thing: raising money — continually. That's what they do. And they hope that all the stars will align — that the VC market cycle will be aligned, that the point in their company's life will be aligned — and when it's all aligned, they raise as much as possible, then they spend it, and then they start all over again.

Good time to raise money. Product is ready, it demos well, it's in beta with 10 healthcare providers who like it. Good inflection point — remember, you have to time all of your activities. The VC market is hot. Bingo. They raise $15 million in a Series B round from three new venture funds at a pre-money valuation of $15 million. They're doing well — it's great. By the way, if anyone here wants to invest in them, you're welcome — I'll take subscriptions afterward.

The round dilutes the founders by 50%, and Joe now owns 13% of the company. That's what happens when people buy portions of your company.

So they have a product in beta and they're getting good feedback, so it's time to start selling. Julie, who is VP of Sales, has her Harvard MBA — I hope there's no Harvard MBA in the room because you might notice my opinion about it. She's in charge of sales, marketing, customer success, operations, and all that good stuff. She starts hiring people and the team grows to about 50 people. Why? Because they have $15 million in the bank and the VCs said grow, grow. And everyone is busy, because moving from 20 people to 50 people is itself a huge task. They're hiring, they're interviewing, they're having meetings, getting to know one another — because for every person you know, there are two and a half people you don't know. So you're really busy, running from meeting to meeting, because 20 people turned into 50. The office is a buzz of activity, tons of stuff going on. Expenses grow to $750,000 a month because 50 people is more expensive than 20 people.

But Joe starts to notice something: a tremendous amount of activity, everyone running from meeting to meeting, everyone is busy — but no results coming out. What's going on here? So he argues with Julie. He says, "We told the board we're going to have a thousand service providers online by the end of the quarter, and we have 100. I have a board meeting next week — what am I going to tell them?" She says, "Don't worry, I'll handle it." He says, "What are you going to tell them? We said 1,000, you put in all of that effort, and we don't have the results to show for it." They're also having a hard time finding people who will pay for the service. Remember, we have two sides to this — we have the service providers, the psychologists and social workers — but to make money, they need to get people who need the service to pay for it, and they take a cut. So tension starts to grow.

Very typical in a company like this is the blame game — "How come you didn't do that?" "Well, it's not my fault." "You had to build this platform and it doesn't work." And so on. Julie launches an expensive campaign to sign up mental health providers and paying clients. That's what you do — you need to get customers, you spend a lot of money, you run a lot of campaigns — but the results are not sufficient, and the tensions grow. The board gets involved and Julie is asked to leave.

Look at all the companies you know and you'll see they all had co-founders who disappeared. Why? Something like this. As the company gets into the real work, it turns out some people deliver and some people don't. If they're just employees, they get fired. If they're co-founders, they are asked to leave. That's what happened here.

חשוב מאוד: השתמשו במה שאתם לומדים על ה-sales funnel, packaging, ונקודות מחיר כדי לבנות מודל מכירות ריאליסטי יותר. ויהיה הרבה יותר קל לגייס כסף. אם אתם באים אליי ואומרים, "הנה מה שעשיתי — הבנתי את השוק הזה, הבנתי איך להגיע אליו, והם הסכימו לשלם 150 דולר לפגישה" — בסדר, עכשיו אני יכול להכפיל אחד בשני ולומר, בסדר, אני יכול לראות שאתם יכולים להרוויח 50,000 דולר בחודש פשוט על ידי הכפלת המספרים. זה נותן לי תחושה טובה יותר.

למה אתם צריכים ממני כסף? ממש, אני שואל את זה כל הזמן — למה אתם צריכים ממני כסף? פשוט לכו ועשו את זה. חלק עשו את זה, והם כבר לא היו צריכים אותי. הם הלכו ועשו את זה בעצמם.

בסדר, אמרתי לכם בהתחלה שאני אסכם בסוף את מה שכיסינו. אז אעבור על זה מהר. הסתכלנו על חיי יזם טיפוסי בפעם הראשונה, תהליך גיוס ההון, המערכת האקולוגית של venture capital, המתמטיקה של גיוס הון. הדבר החשוב ביותר הוא החבל — כשאתם מגייסים כסף, כמה דברים שאתם לא שולטים בהם משחקים תפקיד ביכולת שלכם לגייס כסף. זה ממש חשוב לזכור. דיברנו על למה 9 מתוך 10 חברות נכשלות, ולמה אפילו המספר 10 נכשל. ואחר כך הראיתי לכם את הדרך החכמה יותר.

שאלות? שני דברים — או שזה היה כל כך ברור שאין שאלות, או שלא הקשבתם למילה אחת. תודה רבה.

This lecture, the tenth in SmartUp's Foundations Course, explores one of entrepreneurship's most pressing questions: why do nine out of ten startups fail, and is this outcome inevitable? Delivered by Yonatan Stern, the session argues that startup failure is not a law of nature but the predictable result of ignoring a teachable, repeatable methodology for building successful companies. A successful company, as defined by the SmartUp framework, must be profitable, fast-growing, and able to sustain that growth primarily from internal resources rather than continuous external investment.

To ground the theory in reality, Stern follows the journey of a fictional but representative first-time founder — a talented engineer with a promising idea in the online mental health services space. This case study traces the full arc of startup life: early excitement, the scramble to raise capital, and the gradual loss of control that comes with successive funding rounds. Along the way, Stern demystifies the mechanics of venture capital, explaining pre- and post-money valuations, dilution, and the mathematics behind each funding round. Founders often begin with a healthy ownership stake only to find themselves holding a fraction of the company by the time Series B or C arrives, particularly when investors introduce instruments like Participating Preferred — a clause that allows investors to first recoup their capital and then share proportionally in any remaining upside.

A central theme is the "tightrope walk" inherent in the VC-funded model. Because the company is not yet profitable, it must raise money continuously, making its survival dependent on factors largely outside the founder's control — market sentiment, investor appetite, and timing. Stern illustrates how this pressure distorts decision-making and increases the likelihood of failure.

The alternative, which Stern calls "the smarter way," begins before a single line of code is written or a single hire is made. Founders are urged to validate the market first — experimenting with pricing, packaging, and customer acquisition through rapid, low-cost tests, much like playing a game with fast feedback loops. Only once there is clear evidence that a market exists, that it can be reached, and that customers will pay, should any money be spent on product development. This sequencing dramatically improves the odds of success and allows founders to retain a far larger share of the company they built.

ההרצאה עוסקת בגישה חכמה לבניית סטארטאפ, ומציגה עיקרון מרכזי אחד: יש להפוך את הסדר הרגיל של בניית חברה. במקום לפתח מוצר ורק לאחר מכן לנסות למכור אותו, על היזם להתחיל במכירה מיום הראשון, עוד לפני שהוציא שקל אחד על פיתוח.

המרצה מדגים עיקרון זה דרך פרויקט בשם BBuddy, אפליקציה שנועדה לחבר אנשים הזקוקים לתמיכה רגשית עם "מחברים" טבעיים — אנשים שאחרים נפתחים בפניהם ורוצים לשתף איתם, ושיכולים לספק עצה ותמיכה במחיר נמוך בהרבה מטיפול מקצועי. לפני כל פיתוח טכנולוגי, הצוות הוציא 2,500 דולר בלבד על מודעות פייסבוק, סקרים ושיחות עם לקוחות פוטנציאליים כדי לבדוק אם הרעיון מעשי. כך הם בדקו ביקוש, זיהו קהלי יעד, ולמדו לאיזה מסר אנשים מגיבים — עוד לפני שהיה להם מוצר.

המרצה מסביר שה-pivot — שינוי כיוון עסקי — חייב להתרחש לפני שנוצרות הוצאות קבועות גבוהות, לא אחרי שחברה כבר מוציאה חצי מיליון דולר בחודש. הדרך להימנע מכך היא לדבר עם לקוחות פוטנציאליים מוקדם ככל האפשר ולבנות תהליך שיווקי שיטתי הניתן לסקייל — לא להסתמך על קשרים אישיים שאינם ניתנים להרחבה.

המרצה מבחין בין branding ל-marketing: branding הוא תהליך פסיבי שיוצר מודעות בתודעת הלקוח, בעוד שmarketing הוא תהליך אקטיבי ומדיד שמטרתו לשנות התנהגות ולגרום ללקוח לבצע פעולה. חשוב להשקיע קודם בבניית brand, כי בלעדיו קמפיינים שיווקיים יניבו תוצאות דלות. דוגמה חשובה שעולה מהרצאה: לקוחות רבים, בעיקר בB2B, אינם מודעים כלל לכך שיש להם בעיה — ולפעמים תפקיד המכירה הראשון הוא לשכנע אותם שהבעיה קיימת.

בתחום התמחור, המרצה ממליץ לגבות מחיר גבוה ככל הניתן, משום שזה מאפשר להגיע ליעדי הכנסה עם פחות לקוחות. לצד זאת, חשובה גם אסטרטגיית ה-packaging — פירוק מחזור המכירה לחלקים ויצירת ערך ממשי בכל שלב. בסיכום, המרצה מדגיש שCEO שאינו מתמקד במכירות מרגע ההקמה אינו CEO אמיתי, וכי יזמים שיבנו תחילה מודל מכירות מוכח יגייסו השקעה בקלות רבה יותר.
